catalog_quote: Stress and pitch are not contrastive in Tiang and are very variable in that even the same speaker may utter the same word differently. Figure 2.1 shows the word mémé ‘slippery, to dream’ produced in isolation by the same speaker during elicitation of a word list. Neither dynamic stress (yellow line) nor pitch (blue line) is stable. ... It seems as if words do not have stress or pitch lexically but acquire them through their position in an utterance and intonation. There is a tendency of stressing the last syllable in a word, especially if it is heavy, containing an offglide diphthong, a triphthong or a coda consonant. Words in isolation and at the end of a sentence usually may have stress on the penultimate syllable and falling pitch on the last syllable. audit.reasoning: Quote verified verbatim at the cited pages of the open-access PDF we hold (Sec. 2.5.1 pp. 78-79; Sec. 3.2.2 p. 87; p. 1). The deciding source is a 2023, 734-pp fieldwork reference grammar (PhD thesis) -- the only grammar of the language in Glottolog -- with an explicit, instrumentally illustrated prosody section; the author's own literature review shows no competing stress description exists (earlier work = surveys, wordlists, unpublished SIL mss, a vowel-acoustics working paper). The 'variable / no lexical stress, final-heavy tendency, penult in isolation' coding matches the source text, and Sec. 3.2.2's remark that a phonological word still carries one primary stress somewhere is consistent with it.
